49047.q: Who was the first person at the South Pole?
49047.e: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, on 14 December 1911. Robert Scott arrived about a month later. The station at the South Pole is named after both.
49047.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole.

49048.q: What do the people at the station at the South Pole do?
49048.e: Scientists live at the station. They study, for example, the ice, the weather and the sky.
49048.m: Research is done at the South Pole station.

49049.q: How do scientists usually get to the station at the South Pole?
49049.e: The journey across the ice to the South Pole is very long and difficult. That is why most people fly in planes that have skis and land on the snow.
49049.m: You fly to the South Pole in planes that land on snow.

49050.q: About how long does the sun shine without a break at the South Pole?
49050.e: At the South Pole the sun shines without a break for about half a year. After that it is dark for about half a year.
49050.m: At the South Pole it is light for half a year and dark for half a year.

49051.q: What does the research station at the South Pole stand on?
49051.e: The station stands on the ice of Antarctica, about 2,800 metres above sea level. The ice underneath is very thick.
49051.m: The station at the South Pole stands on a thick layer of ice.

49052.q: Roughly how much of an iceberg is under water?
49052.e: About nine tenths of an iceberg lie under water. You only see the tip.
49052.m: Most of an iceberg is hidden under water.

49053.q: Which famous ship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
49053.e: The Titanic hit an iceberg on the night of 14 to 15 April 1912 and sank a few hours later. Many people died.
49053.m: The Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg.

49054.q: What kind of water is an iceberg made of?
49054.e: Icebergs come from glacier ice. This ice comes from snow, so it is not salty.
49054.m: Icebergs are made of fresh water.

49055.q: Why does an iceberg float in the sea?
49055.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why it floats on top.
49055.m: Ice floats because it is lighter than water.

49056.q: What is it called when a glacier by the sea lets an iceberg break off?
49056.e: When a piece of the glacier breaks off into the sea, people say: the glacier is calving.
49056.m: A glacier calves when an iceberg breaks off.

49057.q: What are the flat, wide icebergs in Antarctica called?
49057.e: In Antarctica flat icebergs often break off the ice shelf. They look like a table and are called tabular icebergs.
49057.m: Tabular icebergs are flat like a table.

49058.q: What happens to an iceberg that drifts into warm sea?
49058.e: In warmer water the iceberg slowly melts. In the end only water is left.
49058.m: In the warm sea an iceberg melts.

49059.q: What does a polar bear often use to find its prey from far away?
49059.e: Polar bears have a very good sense of smell. They can smell seals even under the snow.
49059.m: The polar bear has a very good nose.

49060.q: What do polar bears like to eat most?
49060.e: Polar bears mainly hunt seals on the sea ice. The fatty meat gives them lots of energy.
49060.m: Polar bears like hunting seals best.

49061.q: What colour is a polar bear’s skin?
49061.e: Under its pale fur the polar bear has black skin. Dark skin takes in the sun’s warmth well.
49061.m: A polar bear has black skin under its pale fur.

49062.q: Why is the polar bear well protected from the cold?
a: It always stays in the water
49062.e: The polar bear has thick fur and a thick layer of fat. Both keep it warm.
49062.m: Fur and fat keep the polar bear warm.

49063.q: Where does a polar bear mother give birth to her cubs?
49063.e: In winter the female polar bear digs a den in the snow. The cubs are born there.
49063.m: Polar bear cubs are born in a snow den.

49064.q: Can a polar bear swim well?
49064.e: Polar bears are very good swimmers. They can swim long distances from ice floe to ice floe.

49065.q: Why do polar bears have a hard time when the sea ice melts?
49065.e: Polar bears catch seals from the ice. Without sea ice it is harder for them to find food.
49065.m: Polar bears need the sea ice for hunting.

49066.q: How many cubs does a female polar bear usually have at once?
49066.e: A female polar bear usually has two cubs, sometimes only one. They stay with their mother for more than two years.
49066.m: Female polar bears usually have twins.

49067.e: The emperor penguin is the largest kind of penguin. It grows more than a metre tall.
49067.m: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin.

49068.q: Where does the emperor penguin live?
49068.e: Emperor penguins live only around Antarctica. There are no penguins at the North Pole.
49068.m: Emperor penguins live in the south, in Antarctica.

49069.q: In emperor penguins, who keeps the egg warm?
49069.e: In emperor penguins the father incubates the egg. During this time the mother goes to feed in the sea.
49069.m: In emperor penguins the father keeps the egg warm.

49070.q: Where does an emperor penguin carry its egg while incubating it?
49070.e: The egg rests on the penguin’s feet. A warm fold of skin on its belly covers it.
49070.m: The emperor penguin keeps the egg warm on its feet.

49071.q: What do emperor penguins do when an icy storm comes?
49071.e: Many emperor penguins stand close together and keep each other warm. They keep swapping from the edge to the warm middle.
49071.m: Emperor penguins keep warm by huddling together.

49072.e: Penguins are birds that cannot fly. But they swim very well with their wings.
49072.m: Penguins do not fly; they swim with their wings.

49073.e: Emperor penguins dive in the sea for fish, squid and small crustaceans.
49073.m: Emperor penguins get their food from the sea.

49074.q: What colour is an emperor penguin on its neck?
49074.e: The emperor penguin is black and white. On its neck and ears it has yellow-orange patches.
49074.m: The emperor penguin has yellow patches on its neck.

49075.q: In which season do emperor penguins breed?
49075.e: Emperor penguins breed in the middle of the freezing winter, when it is almost always dark. So the egg has to be kept very warm.
49075.m: Emperor penguins breed in the cold winter.

49076.q: What do seals have instead of legs?
49076.e: Seals have flippers. With them they swim very well in the water.

49077.q: What protects seals from the cold in icy water?
49077.e: Seals have a thick layer of blubber under their skin. It keeps them warm.
49077.m: Blubber keeps seals warm in cold water.

49078.e: The elephant seal is the largest seal. The males have a nose that looks like a short trunk.
49078.m: The elephant seal is the largest seal.

49079.q: Which seal of Antarctica also eats penguins?
49079.e: The leopard seal is a strong hunter in the Southern Ocean. It eats fish, penguins and even other seals.

49080.q: Why do seals make holes in the ice?
49080.e: Seals are mammals and must breathe air. Under the ice they need breathing holes.
49080.m: Seals need air and breathe through holes in the ice.

49081.e: Seals dive in the sea and mainly catch fish. Some also eat squid or crustaceans.

49082.q: Which seals have small ear flaps and can walk on their flippers on land?
49082.e: Sea lions have small ears and can turn their back flippers forwards. That way they walk quite skilfully on land.
49082.m: Sea lions have small ears and walk on their flippers.

49083.q: Which animal group do seals belong to?
49083.e: Seals are mammals. The young drink milk from their mother.

49084.q: What does a walrus have in its mouth that you can see clearly?
49084.e: The walrus has two long tusks. They are extra-long canine teeth.
49084.m: The walrus has two long tusks.

49085.e: Walruses live in the north, in the Arctic. There are no walruses in the Antarctic.
49085.m: Walruses live in the cold north.

49086.q: What does a walrus like to eat most?
49086.e: Walruses search the seabed for clams. They suck the soft insides out of the shell.

49087.q: What is one thing a walrus uses its tusks for?
a: To pull itself onto the ice
49087.e: Walruses dig their tusks into the ice and use them to pull themselves out of the water.
49087.m: The walrus pulls itself onto the ice with its tusks.

49088.q: What does the walrus use to feel for its food on the seabed?
49088.e: The walrus has lots of stiff whiskers. With them it feels for clams in the dark water.
49088.m: The walrus feels with its whiskers.

49089.q: Do both male and female walruses have tusks?
49089.e: Males and females both have tusks. The males’ tusks are usually longer.
49089.m: Both male and female walruses have tusks.

49090.q: How do walruses often lie on the beach or on the ice?
49090.e: Walruses are sociable animals. They often lie close together in big groups.
49090.m: Walruses like lying close together in groups.

49091.e: Despite its German name, which means ‘whale horse’, the walrus is neither a whale nor a horse. It belongs to the seals.
49091.m: The walrus belongs to the seals.

49092.q: What are the northern and southern lights?
a: Colourful lights in the night sky
49092.e: The polar lights are glowing bands and veils in the night sky. They often move like a curtain in the wind.
49092.m: The polar lights glow in colours in the night sky.

49093.q: What colour are the polar lights most often?
49093.e: Most polar lights glow green. Red or purple colours are seen less often.
49093.m: The polar lights usually glow green.

49094.q: What are the polar lights in the north called?
49094.e: Polar lights in the north are called the northern lights. You can see them in Norway, Iceland or Canada, for example.
49094.m: In the north, the polar lights are called the northern lights.

49095.q: Where do the particles that make the polar lights glow come from?
49095.e: The sun hurls tiny particles into space. When they hit the Earth’s air high up, the sky glows.
49095.m: Particles from the sun make the polar lights glow.

49096.q: When can you see the polar lights best?
49096.e: The polar lights are not very bright. You can only see them when the sky is dark and clear.
49096.m: You see the polar lights on clear, dark nights.

49097.q: Can you sometimes see the polar lights in Switzerland too?
49097.e: During strong solar storms you can, rarely, see the polar lights in Switzerland too. This happened in May 2024, for example.
49097.m: Very rarely, the polar lights glow over Switzerland too.

49098.q: Where are the polar lights seen most often?
49098.e: The polar lights mainly appear near the poles. That is why they are called polar lights.
49098.m: The polar lights are seen mainly near the poles.

49099.q: What are the polar lights in the south called?
49099.e: Polar lights around the South Pole are called the southern lights. You can see them in Antarctica or in the south of New Zealand, for example.
49099.m: In the south, the polar lights are called the southern lights.

49100.q: What are the people called who have lived in the Arctic for a long time, for example in Greenland and Canada?
49100.e: The Inuit have lived in the Arctic for centuries. They live in Greenland, Canada, Alaska and Russia.
49100.m: The Inuit are a people of the Arctic.

49101.q: Which narrow boat comes from the Inuit and other peoples of the Arctic?
49101.e: The kayak was developed by peoples of the Arctic such as the Inuit. In the past it was made of wood or bone and animal skin.
49101.m: The kayak is an Inuit boat.

49102.q: Which animals traditionally pull the sledges of the Inuit?
49102.e: In the past the Inuit travelled over ice and snow on dog sledges. Sledge dogs are strong and have lots of stamina.
49102.m: Among the Inuit, dogs pull the sledges.

49103.q: What did the Inuit mainly live on in the past?
49103.e: Hardly any crops grow in the Arctic. That is why the Inuit hunted seals, whales and caribou and caught fish.
49103.m: The Inuit lived by hunting and fishing.

49104.q: Which jacket with a hood gets its name from the Inuit?
49104.e: The word anorak comes from the language of the Inuit. It is a warm jacket with a hood.
49104.m: The word anorak comes from the Inuit.

49105.q: What did the Inuit make their warm clothes from in the past?
49105.e: The Inuit sewed their clothes from the furs and skins of animals. These kept them very warm.
49105.m: The Inuit used to wear clothes made of fur.

49106.q: What is an igloo built from?
49106.e: An igloo is built from firm blocks of snow. The blocks are laid on top of each other in a circle.
49106.m: An igloo is made of blocks of snow.

49107.e: An igloo is round and shaped like a dome, like half a ball.
49107.m: An igloo is round like a dome.

49108.q: Why is it warmer inside an igloo than outside?
49108.e: Snow has lots of air trapped in it. That is why it hardly lets body heat escape.
49108.m: Snow keeps the warmth inside the igloo.

49109.q: What did the Inuit often use an igloo for?
49109.e: Many Inuit built igloos as shelter on long hunting trips in winter. Otherwise they often lived in houses made of stone, earth or animal skins.
49109.m: Igloos were often used as shelter while hunting.

49110.q: Why is the entrance to an igloo often low down like a tunnel?
a: So you can get in faster
49110.e: Cold air is heavy and stays low down. A low entrance keeps it away from the living space.
49110.m: The low entrance keeps the cold outside.

49111.q: Which tool did the Inuit use to cut blocks of snow for an igloo?
49111.e: The Inuit used a long snow knife made of bone, and later of metal. With it they cut the blocks from firm snow.
49111.m: A snow knife cuts the blocks for an igloo.

a: A sheet of ice floating on the sea
49112.e: An ice shelf is a thick sheet of ice. It is attached to the land and floats on the sea.
49112.m: An ice shelf floats on the sea and is attached to the land.

49113.q: Where does the ice of an ice shelf come from?
49113.e: Glaciers flow slowly from the land into the sea. There their ice floats on as an ice shelf.
49113.m: Ice shelves form from glaciers flowing into the sea.

49114.q: Where is most of the shelf ice?
49114.e: There are many large ice shelves around Antarctica. There the ice flows from the continent into the sea.
49114.m: Most shelf ice lies around Antarctica.

49115.q: Roughly how big is the largest ice shelf in Antarctica?
a: About as big as the canton of Zurich
About as big as Lake Constance
49115.e: The Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica is the largest ice shelf in the world. It is about as big as France.
49115.m: The largest ice shelf is about as big as France.

49116.q: How big can an iceberg that breaks off an ice shelf be?
a: Bigger than the canton of Zurich
As big as a football pitch
49116.e: In 2017 the iceberg A68 broke off the Larsen C Ice Shelf. It covered about 5,800 square kilometres, more than three times the size of the canton of Zurich.
49116.m: Huge icebergs can break off ice shelves.

49117.q: Roughly how thick is shelf ice?
49117.e: Shelf ice is usually several hundred metres thick. It is much thicker than sea ice.
49117.m: Shelf ice is many hundreds of metres thick.

49118.q: What does the edge of an ice shelf at the sea often look like?
a: Like a high wall of ice
49118.e: The edge of an ice shelf often rises out of the sea as a steep wall of ice. It can be many metres high.
49118.m: An ice shelf often ends in a high wall of ice.

49119.q: Where was the lowest temperature on Earth measured?
49119.e: The lowest temperature was measured in Antarctica. Antarctica is the coldest continent.

49120.q: Roughly how cold was it when the cold record was set in Antarctica?
49120.e: In 1983, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was measured in Antarctica. That is the lowest air temperature ever measured at a weather station.
49120.m: The cold record is almost minus 90 degrees.

49121.q: Where was the lowest temperature ever recorded at a weather station measured in 1983?
49121.e: At the Russian Vostok Station in Antarctica, about minus 89 degrees was measured in 1983. It lies about 3,500 metres up on the ice.
49121.m: The cold record was measured in Antarctica.

49122.e: The bigger the number after the minus, the colder it is. So minus 40 degrees is the coldest.
49122.m: Minus 40 degrees is colder than minus 10 degrees.

49123.q: In which Antarctic season was the 1983 cold record set?
49123.e: The record was measured in July 1983. In July it is winter in the southern hemisphere.
49123.m: The cold record was measured in the Antarctic winter.

49124.q: Why is it even colder in the Antarctic than in the Arctic?
a: It is high up and covered in thick ice
There are lots of volcanoes there
49124.e: Antarctica is a continent with a thick layer of ice, and it lies high up. In the Arctic, the sea under the ice warms things a little.
49124.m: Antarctica is colder because it is high up and full of ice.

49125.q: What is the area around the South Pole called?
49125.e: The area around the South Pole is called the Antarctic. The continent of Antarctica lies there.
49125.m: The Antarctic is in the very south of the Earth.

49126.q: Do people live in Antarctica their whole lives?
a: No, only scientists for a while
49126.e: There are no cities and no permanent inhabitants in Antarctica. Scientists and their helpers live there in stations for only a few months.
49126.m: People live in Antarctica only for a certain time.

49127.q: What is the sea around Antarctica called?
49127.e: The Southern Ocean lies around Antarctica. It is very cold and partly frozen in winter.
49127.m: Antarctica is surrounded by the Southern Ocean.

49128.q: How far can a big kangaroo get with one jump?
49128.e: Big kangaroos manage up to about 9 metres in one jump. That is as far as two cars one behind the other.
49128.m: Kangaroos can jump a very long way.

49129.q: How big is a baby kangaroo when it is born?
a: About as big as a bean
About as big as a cat
About as big as an apple
About as big as a dog
49129.e: A newborn kangaroo is only about 2 to 3 centimetres long and weighs less than 1 gram. After that it keeps growing for many months.
49129.m: A baby kangaroo is tiny when it is born.

49130.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
49130.e: A young kangaroo is called a ‘joey’. A puppy is a young dog, a kitten a young cat and a chick a young bird.
49130.m: A baby kangaroo is called a joey.

49131.q: How do kangaroos move forward quickly?
49131.e: Kangaroos jump with their powerful back legs. That way they move fast and far.
49131.m: Kangaroos hop with their strong back legs.

49132.q: What does the kangaroo need its thick, long tail for?
49132.e: When jumping, the tail keeps it balanced. When standing, the kangaroo also leans on it.
49132.m: The tail helps the kangaroo keep its balance.

49133.e: Kangaroos are plant eaters. They mainly eat grasses, herbs and leaves.

49134.q: How do male kangaroos fight each other?
49134.e: Male kangaroos stand up and box with their front legs. They lean on their tail and kick with their back legs.

49135.q: Which is the largest marsupial in the world?
49135.e: The red kangaroo is the largest marsupial alive today. A male standing upright can be as tall as a person.
49135.m: The red kangaroo is the largest marsupial.

49136.q: In which country does the koala live?
49136.e: Koalas live only in the east and south-east of Australia. There they live in eucalyptus forests.

49137.q: Where does the koala get most of its water from?
49137.e: Koalas rarely drink. Most of their water is in the moist leaves they eat.
49137.m: The koala gets its water from the leaves.

49138.q: The koala looks like a small bear. What is it really?
49138.e: The koala is sometimes called the koala bear, but it is not a bear. It is a marsupial; its young grow up in a pouch.
49138.m: The koala is not a bear but a marsupial.

49139.q: Where does the koala spend most of its time?
49139.e: Koalas are very good climbers and almost always live in trees. They only come down to the ground to move to the next tree.

49140.q: About how long does a koala sleep or doze each day?
49140.e: Koalas sleep and doze for up to 20 hours a day, usually snugly in the fork of a branch.
49140.m: The koala sleeps almost all day.

49141.q: Why does the koala sleep so much?
a: It hunts for a long time at night
49141.e: Eucalyptus leaves contain few nutrients and are hard to digest. That is why the koala saves energy by sleeping a lot.
49141.m: Eucalyptus gives the koala only a little energy.

49142.q: What colour is the koala’s fur usually?
49142.e: The koala’s thick, soft fur is grey to greyish brown. It is lighter on the belly.

49143.q: What about the koala’s fingers is very similar to a human’s?
49143.e: Koalas have fingerprints that look very much like human ones. This is very rare in animals.
49143.m: The koala has fingerprints like a human.

49144.q: What does the koala use to hold on tightly to branches?
49144.e: Koalas have strong paws with sharp claws. With them they cling safely to trunks and branches.
49144.m: The koala climbs with sharp claws.

49145.q: On which continent do most lions live?
49145.e: Almost all wild lions live in Africa south of the Sahara.

49146.q: How can you recognise an adult male lion straight away?
49146.e: Male lions have a big mane around their head and neck. Lionesses have no mane.
49146.m: The male lion has a mane.

49147.q: Who usually does the hunting in a pride of lions?
49147.e: Usually the females hunt together. The males mainly protect the territory.
49147.m: In a pride, the lionesses usually hunt.

49148.q: What is the lion often called?
49148.e: Because of its strength and its mane, the lion is often called the ‘king of the animals’.
49148.m: The lion is often called the king of the animals.

49149.q: In which landscape do lions usually live?
49149.e: Lions live mainly in the savannah. That is open grassland with scattered trees.

49150.q: Which animals do lions hunt, for example?
49150.e: Lions are meat eaters. They hunt large animals such as zebras, wildebeest and antelopes.
49150.m: Lions hunt large animals such as zebras.

49151.q: In which country in Asia do wild lions still live?
49151.e: A small group of Asiatic lions still lives in the Gir Forest in the west of India. Elsewhere in Asia, lions have disappeared.
49151.m: Wild Asiatic lions still live in India.

49152.q: On which two continents do wild elephants live?
49152.e: There are African elephants and Asian elephants. No wild elephants live on other continents.
49152.m: Elephants live in Africa and Asia.

49153.q: What is the elephant’s long nose called?
49153.e: The trunk is the nose and upper lip together. It is very flexible and strong.
49153.m: The elephant’s nose is called a trunk.

49154.q: What are the elephant’s long teeth called?
49154.e: Tusks are very long incisor teeth. They are made of ivory.

49155.q: How long does a female elephant carry her baby before it is born?
49155.e: A female elephant is pregnant for about 22 months, so almost two years. That is the longest pregnancy of any land animal.
49155.m: A baby elephant grows in its mother for almost two years.

49156.q: Which elephant has the bigger ears?
49156.e: African elephants have very big ears. The ears of Asian elephants are clearly smaller.

49157.q: What is a baby elephant called?
49157.e: A young elephant is called a calf. It stays with its mother and the herd for many years.
49157.m: A young elephant is called a calf.

49158.q: Why do elephants flap their big ears?
49158.e: There are lots of blood vessels in the ears. Flapping cools the blood, so the elephant feels less hot.
49158.m: Elephants cool down with their ears.

49159.e: Elephants are plant eaters. They eat grass, leaves, bark and fruit, a huge amount every day.

49160.q: Who leads a herd of elephants?
49160.e: An experienced older female leads the herd. She knows the way to water and food.
49160.m: An old female elephant leads the herd.

49161.e: Unlike many other bears, the giant panda does not hibernate. It eats bamboo in winter too.
49161.m: The giant panda does not hibernate.

49162.q: What does the giant panda eat almost exclusively?
49162.e: The giant panda eats almost nothing but bamboo. It needs a huge amount of it every day.

49163.q: What colours is the giant panda’s fur?
49163.e: The giant panda is black and white. The ears, the legs and the patches around the eyes are black, for example.
49163.m: The giant panda is black and white.

49164.q: In which landscape does the giant panda live?
49164.e: Pandas live in cool, damp mountain forests where lots of bamboo grows.
49164.m: The panda lives in mountain forests with bamboo.

49165.q: What helps the giant panda hold the bamboo?
49165.e: The panda has an extra-long bone on its front paw. It works like an extra thumb.
49165.m: An extra thumb helps the panda hold things.

49166.q: About how long does a giant panda spend eating each day?
49166.e: Bamboo gives little energy. That is why the panda eats for many hours every day, often more than ten.
49166.m: The panda eats for many hours a day.

49167.q: Which animal is in the logo of the nature conservation organisation WWF?
49167.e: Since it was founded in 1961, the WWF has had a giant panda in its logo. The WWF was founded in Switzerland.
49167.m: The panda is the symbol of the WWF.

49168.q: Roughly how much does a baby panda weigh at birth?
49168.e: A newborn panda weighs only about 100 grams. That is as light as a bar of chocolate.
49168.m: A baby panda is tiny at birth.

49169.q: In which country do most wild tigers live today?
49169.e: More than half of all wild tigers live in India. There are many protected areas for tigers there.
49169.m: Most wild tigers live in India.

49170.q: What does a tiger’s fur look like?
49170.e: Tigers have orange fur with black stripes. This camouflages them well in tall grass and in the forest.

49171.q: Which is the largest cat in the world?
49171.e: The tiger is the largest kind of cat. It is even a bit bigger and heavier than the lion.
49171.m: The tiger is the largest cat.

49172.q: What do tigers like, unlike many other cats?
49172.e: Tigers are good swimmers. On hot days they like lying in the water.

49173.q: How does an adult tiger usually live?
49173.e: Tigers are loners. Each tiger has its own territory.

49174.q: Which tiger lives mainly in India?
49174.e: The Bengal tiger is also called the royal Bengal tiger. It lives mainly in India and in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh and Nepal.
49174.m: The Bengal tiger lives in India.

49175.q: Which tiger lives in the cold, snowy east of Russia?
49175.e: The Siberian tiger, also called the Amur tiger, lives in the east of Russia. Its thick fur protects it from the cold.
49175.m: The Siberian tiger lives in cold Russia.

49176.q: What is unique about every tiger?
49176.e: No tiger has the same stripes as another. Tigers can be recognised by them.
49176.m: Every tiger has its own stripe pattern.

49177.q: When does the tiger usually hunt?
49177.e: Tigers usually hunt at dusk and at night. They creep up and take their prey by surprise.

49178.q: On which continent does the American bison live?
49178.e: The American bison lives in North America, mainly in the USA and Canada.
49178.m: The bison lives in North America.

49179.q: What other name is the American bison often given?
49179.e: Many people call the bison a ‘buffalo’. Strictly speaking, though, the bison is not a true buffalo.
49179.m: The bison is often called a buffalo.

49180.q: Which is the largest land animal in North America?
49180.e: A bison bull can weigh almost a tonne. No other land mammal in North America is so big.
49180.m: The bison is the largest land animal in North America.

49181.q: What does the bison mainly eat?
49181.e: Bison are plant eaters. They mainly eat grasses and herbs.

49182.q: In which landscape did huge herds of bison live in the past?
49182.e: The prairie is a wide grassland in North America. Millions of bison used to roam there.

49183.q: What was the situation of the bison in North America around 1900?
a: There were more than ever before
They had all become farm animals
They had moved to South America
49183.e: In the 19th century millions of bison were hunted. By around 1900 only a few hundred were left; after that they were protected.
49183.m: The bison almost died out around 1900.

49184.q: What does the bison have over its shoulders?
49184.e: The bison has a tall hump of strong muscles over its shoulders. That is why it looks very powerful at the front.
49184.m: The bison has a hump over its shoulders.

49185.q: What is a male bison called?
49185.e: A male bison is called a bull, a female a cow. The young is called a calf.
49185.m: A male bison is called a bull.

49186.q: What is a young bison called?
49186.e: A young bison is called a calf, just like a young cow. It can walk soon after it is born.
49186.m: A young bison is called a calf.

49187.q: Which continent does the llama come from?
49187.e: The llama comes from South America. People there have kept it for thousands of years.
49187.m: The llama comes from South America.

49188.q: How many toes does a llama have on each foot?
49188.e: Llamas have two toes with claws and soft soles on each foot. With them they walk safely on stony mountain paths.
49188.m: The llama has two toes on each foot.

49189.q: What do llamas do when they are annoyed?
49189.e: Llamas spit when they are annoyed or feel threatened. But usually they spit at other llamas.

49190.q: What do people in the Andes often use llamas for?
49190.e: Llamas are good pack animals. They carry goods over steep mountain paths, and their wool is used too.
49190.m: Llamas carry loads in the mountains.

49191.q: Which animal is the llama related to?
49191.e: Llamas belong to the camel family. They are also called New World camels.
49191.m: The llama is related to the camel.

49192.q: Which smaller animal is related to the llama and has especially fine wool?
49192.e: The alpaca is smaller than the llama. It is kept mainly for its soft wool.
49192.m: The alpaca has especially fine wool.

49193.q: Does the llama have a hump like a camel?
49193.e: Llamas are related to camels, but they have no hump. Their back is straight.

49194.q: Which wild animal is the llama descended from?
49194.e: The llama was bred from the wild guanaco a long time ago. The guanaco still lives in South America today.
49194.m: The llama is descended from the guanaco.

49195.q: In which of these countries are there many llamas?
49195.e: Peru lies in the Andes in South America. Especially many llamas live there and in neighbouring Bolivia.
49195.m: There are many llamas in Peru.

49196.q: How heavy can a big Andean condor be?
a: As heavy as a small child
49196.e: A big male weighs up to about 15 kilograms. That is about as much as a three-year-old child.
49196.m: The Andean condor is a very heavy bird.

49197.q: Which group of birds does the Andean condor belong to?
49197.e: The Andean condor is a vulture. It is one of the New World vultures of America.
49197.m: The Andean condor is a vulture.

49198.q: What does the Andean condor mainly eat?
49198.e: The Andean condor eats carrion, that is, dead animals. That way it helps keep nature clean.
49198.m: The Andean condor eats dead animals.

49199.q: Roughly how wide is the wingspan of the Andean condor?
49199.e: With its wings spread, the Andean condor measures up to just over 3 metres. It is one of the largest birds that can fly.
49199.m: The Andean condor has huge wings.

49200.q: How does the Andean condor usually fly?
a: It only flies a short way
49200.e: The Andean condor is heavy. That is why it lets warm, rising air carry it and hardly flaps its wings.
49200.m: The Andean condor glides on rising air.

49201.q: What does the Andean condor’s head look like?
49201.e: The Andean condor’s head has no feathers. That way it stays clean when the bird eats carrion.
49201.m: The Andean condor has a bald head.

49202.q: What does the Andean condor have around its neck?
49202.e: On its neck the Andean condor has a collar of white feathers. Otherwise its plumage is mainly black.
49202.m: The Andean condor has a white neck ruff.

49203.q: On which country’s coat of arms can you see the Andean condor?
49203.e: The Andean condor is on the coat of arms of Chile. Bolivia, Ecuador and Colombia also show it on theirs.
49203.m: The Andean condor is on the coat of arms of Chile.

49204.q: How many eggs does a female Andean condor usually lay at a time?
49204.e: The female usually lays only a single egg, and only every two years. That is why there are few young.
49204.m: The Andean condor lays only one egg.

49205.q: What colour are the feathers of most kiwis?
49205.e: Most kiwis have brown to greyish-brown feathers. That way they are well camouflaged on the forest floor.

49206.e: The kiwi has only tiny wings and cannot fly. It walks around on the ground.

49207.q: When is the kiwi mainly out and about?
49207.e: Kiwis are nocturnal. During the day they sleep in burrows or under thick plants.
49207.m: The kiwi is out and about at night.

a: At the tip of its beak
49208.e: The kiwi is the only bird with nostrils right at the front of its beak. That way it can smell worms in the ground.
49208.m: The kiwi has its nostrils at the tip of its beak.

49209.q: What does the kiwi mainly eat?
49209.e: The kiwi pokes about in the ground with its long beak. There it finds worms, beetles and larvae.
49209.m: The kiwi eats worms and insects.

49210.q: What are people from New Zealand often called?
49210.e: New Zealanders often call themselves ‘Kiwis’, after their country’s famous bird.
49210.m: New Zealanders are often called Kiwis.

49211.q: What is special about the kiwi’s egg?
a: It is very big for the bird
It is smaller than a pea
49211.e: Compared with its body, the kiwi’s egg is huge. It weighs about a fifth as much as the female.
49211.m: The kiwi lays a huge egg.

49212.q: What do the kiwi’s feathers feel like?
49212.e: The kiwi’s feathers are thin and soft. They look more like a coat of hair.
49212.m: The kiwi’s feathers are like hair.

49213.q: Roughly how big is a kiwi?
49213.e: A kiwi is about as big as a farm chicken. It has a round body and short, strong legs.
49213.m: A kiwi is about as big as a chicken.

49214.e: The platypus lives in the east of Australia and on the island of Tasmania.

49215.q: What does the platypus’s bill look like?
49215.e: The platypus has a wide, flat bill. It looks like a duck’s, but it is soft.
49215.m: The platypus has a bill like a duck.

49216.q: What is special about the platypus, even though it is a mammal?
49216.e: Almost all mammals give birth to live young. But the platypus lays eggs.
49216.m: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.

49217.q: What do male platypuses have on their back legs?
49217.e: Males have a spur with venom on their back legs. A sting is very painful for people.
49217.m: The male platypus has a venomous spur.

49218.q: Where does the platypus look for its food?
49218.e: The platypus dives in streams and rivers. There it searches the bottom for small crustaceans, worms and larvae.
49218.m: The platypus looks for its food in the water.

49219.q: Which animal does the platypus’s wide, flat tail look like?
49219.e: The tail is wide and flat like a beaver’s. The platypus stores fat in it.
49219.m: The platypus has a tail like a beaver.

49220.q: How does the platypus find its prey underwater?
49220.e: When diving, the platypus closes its eyes and ears. Its sensitive bill senses the prey.
49220.m: The platypus finds prey with its bill.

49221.q: What does the platypus have on its feet?
49221.e: The platypus has webbing between its toes. That way it can swim well.

49222.q: How do young platypuses drink milk?
a: They lick it from the fur
49222.e: The platypus has no teats. The milk comes out of the skin on the belly, and the young lick it up.
49222.m: Young platypuses lick the milk from the fur.

49223.q: Where does the platypus sleep during the day?
a: In a burrow on the bank
On a rock in the sea
49223.e: With its claws the platypus digs tunnels into the banks of streams and lakes. It rests there during the day.
49223.m: The platypus lives in a burrow on the bank.

49224.q: Which big lake lies west of the Serengeti?
49224.e: Lake Victoria lies west of the Serengeti. It is the largest lake in Africa.
49224.m: Lake Victoria lies west of the Serengeti.

49225.q: On which continent is the Serengeti?
49225.e: The Serengeti is a large grassland in East Africa.
49225.m: The Serengeti is part of Africa.

49226.q: What does the landscape of the Serengeti usually look like?
49226.e: The Serengeti is a wide, flat plain with grass and scattered trees. A landscape like this is called savannah.
49226.m: Mainly grass grows in the Serengeti.

49227.q: What does the name ‘Serengeti’ roughly mean?
49227.e: The name comes from the language of a herding people in East Africa. It roughly means ‘endless plain’.
49227.m: Serengeti means something like endless plain.

49228.q: Which people live with their herds of cattle on the edge of the Serengeti?
49228.e: The Maasai are a herding people in Tanzania and Kenya. They mainly keep cattle.
49228.m: The Maasai are herders in East Africa.

49229.q: Which nature reserve in Kenya borders the Serengeti to the north?
49229.e: The Masai Mara in Kenya joins directly onto the Serengeti. The animals move back and forth between the two areas.
49229.m: The Masai Mara is the Serengeti’s neighbour.

49230.q: Which famous crater full of animals lies right next to the Serengeti?
49230.e: The Ngorongoro Crater is a huge, old volcanic crater. It lies to the south-east of the Serengeti, and a great many animals live on its floor.
49230.m: The Ngorongoro Crater lies next to the Serengeti.

49231.q: Which spotted predators with a call like laughter live in the Serengeti?
49231.e: Many spotted hyenas live in the Serengeti. Their calls sometimes sound like loud giggling or laughing.
49231.m: Spotted hyenas live in the Serengeti.

a: A large national park with savannah in Africa
49232.e: The Serengeti is a wide grassland in Tanzania. Since 1951 it has been a national park where millions of large animals live.
49232.m: The Serengeti is a savannah national park in Africa.

49233.q: Which animals take part most in the Great Migration in the Serengeti?
49233.e: In the Great Migration, huge herds of wildebeest move across the savannah. Other grazers such as gazelles go along too.
49233.m: Most of the migrating animals are wildebeest.

49234.q: Why do the wildebeest migrate every year?
a: They are looking for fresh grass
49234.e: The wildebeest follow the rain. Where it has rained, fresh grass grows for them to eat.
49234.m: The wildebeest follow the rain and the fresh grass.

49235.q: Roughly how many wildebeest take part in the Great Migration?
49235.e: There are well over a million wildebeest. The Great Migration is one of the biggest animal migrations in the world.
49235.m: More than a million wildebeest are on the move.

49236.q: Which river do the wildebeest have to cross on their migration?
49236.e: The Mara flows through Kenya and Tanzania. Crossing it is very dangerous for the wildebeest.
49236.m: The wildebeest swim across the Mara.

49237.q: Which animals lie in wait for the wildebeest in the river?
49237.e: Large Nile crocodiles live in the Mara River. They grab wildebeest swimming through the water.
49237.m: Crocodiles wait in the river for the wildebeest.

49238.q: Which striped animals often migrate together with the wildebeest?
49238.e: Zebras and wildebeest often travel together. The zebras eat the tall grass, the wildebeest the shorter grass underneath.

49239.q: When are most wildebeest calves born?
a: Almost all within a few weeks
49239.e: Most wildebeest calves are born within a few weeks in the rainy season in the south of the Serengeti. Together they are better protected.
49239.m: Many wildebeest calves are born at the same time.

49240.q: How quickly can a newborn wildebeest calf stand up?
49240.e: A wildebeest calf stands up just a few minutes after it is born. Soon afterwards it can run along with the herd.
49240.m: Wildebeest calves stand up very quickly.

49241.q: Roughly what route does the Great Migration follow?
49241.e: Every year the herds move in a big circle between the Serengeti and the Masai Mara. Then the journey starts again.
49241.m: The migration goes round in a circle every year.

49242.e: Zebras have black and white stripes. The pattern covers the whole body.
49242.m: Zebras have black and white stripes.

49243.q: Which animal is the zebra closely related to?
49243.e: Like horses and donkeys, zebras belong to the horse family.
49243.m: The zebra is a relative of the horse.

49244.q: What does a zebra mainly eat?
49244.e: Zebras are plant eaters. They mainly eat grass and spend many hours a day grazing.

49245.q: What is special about the stripes of each zebra?
49245.e: No two zebras have exactly the same stripes. The pattern is as unique as a person’s fingerprint.
49245.m: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern.

49246.q: What is a young zebra called?
49246.e: Like young horses, young zebras are called foals.
49246.m: A baby zebra is called a foal.

49247.e: Zebras live in groups and herds. Together they notice enemies more quickly.

49248.q: What colour is a zebra’s skin under its fur?
49248.e: Under its striped coat, a zebra’s skin is dark.

49249.q: How many species of zebra are there today?
49249.e: There are the plains zebra, Grévy’s zebra and the mountain zebra. The plains zebra lives in the Serengeti.
49249.m: There are three species of zebra.

49250.q: What does a zebra do when a lion attacks?
49250.e: Zebras run away fast. When they are attacked, they can kick hard with their hooves.
49250.m: Zebras flee or defend themselves with kicks.

49251.e: Rhinos are plant eaters. Depending on the species, they eat grass or leaves and twigs.

49252.q: Which two species of rhino live in Africa?
49252.e: The white rhino and the black rhino live in Africa. The other rhinos live in Asia.
49252.m: In Africa there are white and black rhinos.

49253.q: How many horns do African rhinos have?
49253.e: White and black rhinos have two horns, one behind the other. The front one is usually longer.

a: Poachers hunt them for their horns
49254.e: Poachers illegally kill rhinos to sell their horns for a lot of money. That is why rhinos are seriously endangered.
49254.m: Rhinos are poached for their horns.

49255.e: Rhinos see rather badly. But they can smell and hear very well.
49255.m: Rhinos smell better than they see.

49256.q: What is a young rhino called?
49256.e: A young rhino is called a calf. It stays with its mother for a few years.
49256.m: A baby rhino is called a calf.

49257.q: Which bird often sits on the backs of rhinos?
49257.e: Oxpeckers pick ticks and other small creatures out of rhinos’ skin. When danger threatens, they fly up calling loudly.
49257.m: The oxpecker likes sitting on rhinos.

49258.q: Which rhino is the largest in Africa?
49258.e: The white rhino is the largest rhino and, after the elephant, one of the largest land animals.
49258.m: The white rhino is the largest rhino.

49259.q: Which animal is the tallest animal in the world?
49259.e: Giraffes grow more than 5 metres tall. No other animal is so tall.
49259.m: The giraffe is the tallest animal in the world.

49260.q: What colour is a giraffe’s tongue?
49260.e: A giraffe’s long tongue is dark, almost bluish black. This probably protects it from sunburn.
49260.m: The giraffe has a dark tongue.

49261.q: How does a giraffe drink at the water?
a: It spreads its front legs wide
It lies flat on its belly
It only drinks dew from the leaves
It sucks up the water with a trunk
49261.e: Because its legs are so long, the giraffe has to spread its front legs wide to lower its head to the water.
49261.m: When drinking, the giraffe spreads its legs.

49262.q: What does a giraffe have on its head?
49262.e: Giraffes have short, fur-covered horns on their head. They are called ossicones.

49263.q: What happens to a baby giraffe when it is born?
a: It is born in a nest
49263.e: The mother gives birth standing up. So the baby falls from a height of almost 2 metres, which does not harm it.
49263.m: Baby giraffes drop to the ground when they are born.

49264.q: What is special about the coat pattern of each giraffe?
49264.e: The patches of every giraffe are unique. No pattern is exactly like another.
49264.m: Every giraffe has its own patch pattern.

49265.q: What did the word ‘safari’ originally mean?
49265.e: ‘Safari’ comes from Swahili, a language of East Africa. The word means ‘journey’.

49266.q: What do you usually travel through the national park in on a safari?
49266.e: On a safari you usually travel in a sturdy off-road vehicle over bumpy tracks.
49266.m: On safari you travel in an off-road vehicle.

49267.q: What is a national park in Africa mainly for?
49267.e: In a national park, animals and plants are protected. Hunting is not allowed there.
49267.m: A national park protects animals and nature.

49268.q: Which animal is one of the ‘Big Five’ of a safari?
49268.e: The ‘Big Five’ are the lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo and rhino.
49268.m: The leopard is one of the Big Five.

49269.q: When do you often see especially many animals on a safari?
a: Early in the morning and in the evening
49269.e: In the midday heat many animals rest in the shade. In the cool morning and evening they are more active and easier to see.
49269.m: On safari you see many animals in the morning and evening.

49270.q: What should you do on a safari in a national park?
49270.e: Wild animals can be dangerous. That is why you stay in the vehicle and keep your distance.
49270.m: On safari you stay in the car.

49271.q: What is the name of a well-known national park in South Africa?
49271.e: Kruger National Park is the best-known national park in South Africa. All the Big Five animals live there.
49271.m: Kruger National Park is in South Africa.

49272.q: Who goes with visitors in a national park and knows the animals?
49272.e: Rangers work in the national park. They protect the animals and guide visitors. Hunting is not allowed in the national park.
49272.m: Rangers know and protect the animals in the park.

49273.q: Which device helps you see faraway animals clearly on safari?
49273.e: With binoculars you can see animals that are far away large and clear.
49273.m: With binoculars you can see animals in the distance.

49274.q: What is another name for the baobab?
49274.e: The baobab is also called the monkey-bread tree. Its fruit is eaten by baboons, for example.
49274.m: The baobab is also called the monkey-bread tree.

49275.q: What does the baobab store in its thick trunk?
49275.e: The baobab’s thick trunk stores a lot of water. That way the tree survives long dry seasons.
49275.m: The baobab stores water in its trunk.

49276.q: How old can a baobab get?
49276.e: Baobabs grow slowly. Some trees live for more than 1,000 years; the oldest known one was about 2,400 years old.
49276.m: Baobabs can live for more than a thousand years.

49277.q: Why is the baobab sometimes called the ‘upside-down tree’?
49277.e: When the baobab has no leaves, its bare branches look like roots sticking up into the sky.
49277.m: Without leaves, the baobab’s branches look like roots.

49278.q: Roughly how long is a baobab fruit?
49278.e: Baobab fruits are long, have a hard shell and grow about 15 to 25 centimetres long. The flesh is edible.
49278.m: The baobab has large, long fruits.

49279.q: When does the baobab lose its leaves?
49279.e: In the dry season the baobab sheds its leaves. That way it loses less water.
49279.m: The baobab sheds its leaves in the dry season.

49280.q: Which large animal sometimes eats the bark of the baobab?
49280.e: In dry seasons elephants tear bark and wood off the baobab because it contains a lot of water.
49280.m: Elephants sometimes feed on the baobab.

49281.q: When does the baobab bloom with its large white flowers?
49281.e: The large white flowers open in the late afternoon and bloom through the night. Bats help pollinate them.

49282.q: What is a waterhole in the savannah?
a: A place with drinking water for animals
49282.e: Water collects at a waterhole. Many animals come there to drink.

49283.q: When are waterholes especially important for the animals?
49283.e: In the dry season it hardly rains for months. Then there is often water only at a few waterholes.
49283.m: In the dry season waterholes are vital.

49284.q: Why do lions sometimes wait near a waterhole?
49284.e: All animals have to drink. That is why predators lie in wait for prey near waterholes.
49284.m: Predators lie in wait at the waterhole too.

49285.q: What are the two seasons in the savannah called?
49285.e: The savannah has a rainy season and a dry season. Instead of cold and warm, it changes between wet and dry.
49285.m: In the savannah, the rainy season and the dry season take turns.

49286.q: How does an elephant drink at the waterhole?
a: It sucks water into its trunk
49286.e: The elephant sucks water into its trunk. Then it squirts it into its mouth.
49286.m: Elephants drink with the help of their trunk.

49287.q: How can elephants find water in the dry season?
a: They dig in the dry riverbed
49287.e: Elephants dig in the dried-up riverbed with their feet, trunk and tusks. That way they reach water in the ground.

49288.q: Why do zebras and wildebeest like to drink at the waterhole in large groups?
a: They want to learn to swim
49288.e: When drinking, the animals lower their heads and are not paying attention. In a group, there is always one animal that notices when a predator comes.
49288.m: Animals at the waterhole are safer in a group.

49289.q: Why do some animals wallow in the mud at the waterhole?
49289.e: Mud cools the skin and protects it from the hot sun. That is why warthogs and buffalo like to wallow.
49289.m: A mud bath cools you down in the heat.

49290.q: In which landscape can the cheetah hunt best?
49290.e: The cheetah needs a clear view and lots of space for its fast sprint. That is why it prefers to hunt in open grassland.
49290.m: The cheetah prefers to hunt in open grassland.

49291.q: About how fast can a cheetah run?
49291.e: For a short time a cheetah reaches about 100 kilometres per hour. That makes it the fastest land animal in the world.
49291.m: A cheetah runs about as fast as a car on the motorway.

49292.q: How long can a cheetah run that fast?
49292.e: The cheetah is a sprinter. After a few hundred metres it is exhausted and has to rest.
49292.m: The cheetah runs fast, but only for a short time.

49293.q: What does a cheetah have on its face?
49293.e: A cheetah has black stripes running from its eyes to its mouth. They look like tear tracks.

49294.q: When does the cheetah usually hunt?
a: In the middle of the night
49294.e: Cheetahs usually hunt during the day, often in the morning or late afternoon. At night lions and hyenas are out and about.
49294.m: The cheetah hunts during the day.

49295.q: What prey does a cheetah often hunt?
49295.e: Cheetahs mainly hunt medium-sized, fast animals such as gazelles and impalas.

49296.q: What pattern does a cheetah's fur have?
49296.e: The cheetah has yellowish fur with lots of small, solid black spots.

49297.q: What helps the cheetah not to fall over when running round bends?
49297.e: The cheetah uses its long tail like a rudder. It helps it keep its balance on fast turns.
49297.m: The tail helps the cheetah steer.

49298.q: In which country is the Okavango Delta?
49298.e: The Okavango Delta is in the north of Botswana in southern Africa.
49298.m: The Okavango Delta is in Botswana.

49299.q: What is special about the Okavango River?
a: It does not flow into the sea
49299.e: The Okavango does not flow into the sea. Its water spreads out in the delta, seeps away and evaporates.
49299.m: The Okavango never reaches the sea.

49300.q: Which desert borders the Okavango Delta?
49300.e: The Okavango Delta lies in the middle of the Kalahari region. The plentiful water in the dry area attracts animals.
49300.m: The Okavango Delta is a water oasis in the Kalahari.

49301.q: Which boat do people in the Okavango Delta often use?
49301.e: In the delta people travel in narrow dugout canoes called mokoro. They are pushed along with a long pole.
49301.m: In the Okavango Delta people travel by dugout canoe.

49302.q: What does the Okavango Delta look like?
49302.e: In the delta the river splits into many small channels. Between them are islands, swamps and grassland.
49302.m: The Okavango Delta is made up of many channels and islands.

49303.q: What is special about the Okavango River in Africa?
49303.e: The Okavango flows into the Kalahari and branches out there into a huge inland delta. There its water seeps away and evaporates. Since 2014 the delta has been a World Heritage Site.
49303.m: The Okavango ends in a delta in the middle of the land.

49304.q: Which large animals live in especially large numbers in the Okavango Delta area?
49304.e: A great many elephants live in the north of Botswana. They like to come to the water in the delta.
49304.m: Lots of elephants live in the Okavango Delta.

49305.q: When does the Okavango Delta have the most water?
49305.e: The rainwater from Angola takes months to reach the delta. That is why the delta is fullest in, of all times, the dry season.
49305.m: The Okavango Delta is fullest in the dry season.

49306.q: Where does a hippo usually spend the hot day?
49306.e: Hippos lie in the water during the day. That keeps their sensitive skin moist and cool.
49306.m: Hippos spend the day in the water.

49307.e: Hippos are plant-eaters. They mainly eat grass, and lots of it.

49308.q: When does the hippo go on land to feed?
49308.e: At night hippos leave the water. They often walk for kilometres to eat grass.
49308.m: Hippos feed on land at night.

49309.q: What other name does the hippo have?
49309.e: The hippo's full name is hippopotamus. It lives in the rivers and lakes of Africa.
49309.m: The hippo is also called the hippopotamus.

49310.q: What protects the hippo's skin from the sun?
49310.e: Hippos produce a reddish liquid on their skin. It works like sun cream.
49310.m: Hippos have their own sun protection.

49311.q: How does a hippo often move about underwater?
49311.e: Hippos are heavy and hardly swim properly. They walk or bounce along the bottom underwater.
49311.m: Hippos walk along the bottom underwater.

49312.q: What can you often only see when a hippo is lying in the water?
49312.e: The eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of the head. So the hippo can go almost completely underwater and still breathe and look around.
49312.m: With a hippo, only the eyes, ears and nose stick out of the water.

49313.q: Is the hippo a harmless animal?
49313.e: Hippos defend their territory fiercely and can attack very quickly. They are among the most dangerous animals in Africa.

49314.q: Which animals are the hippo's closest relatives?
49314.e: Although its name means “river horse”, the hippo is not related to the horse. Its closest living relatives are whales.
49314.m: The hippo is related to whales.

49315.q: What does a hippo show when it opens its mouth wide?
49315.e: A hippo opens its mouth very wide and shows its long canine teeth. That is how it threatens other animals.
49315.m: With its mouth open wide, the hippo is making a threat.

49316.q: What sounds does a cheetah make?
49316.e: The cheetah cannot roar. It purrs like a pet cat and makes chirping sounds, almost like a bird.
49316.m: The cheetah purrs, but it does not roar.

49317.q: About how tall is a baby giraffe at birth?
49317.e: A newborn giraffe is about 1.8 metres tall and weighs around 50 kilograms. So it is taller than most adults.
49317.m: Even a baby giraffe is very tall.

49318.q: About how thick is a rhino's skin?
49318.e: A rhino's skin is very thick, in some places up to about 5 centimetres. It works like armour.

49319.q: About how many individual reefs make up the Great Barrier Reef?
49319.e: The Great Barrier Reef is not one single reef. It is made up of about 2,900 individual reefs and many small islands.
49319.m: The Great Barrier Reef is made up of thousands of reefs.

49320.q: Which large whales come to the Great Barrier Reef every year to have their young?
49320.e: In winter humpback whales swim from the cold seas in the south to the warm reef. There they give birth to their young.
49320.m: Humpback whales have their young in the warm water near the reef.

49321.q: Which sea cow eats seagrass near the Great Barrier Reef?
49321.e: The dugong is a sea cow. It eats seagrass in the meadows in the shallow water near the reef.
49321.m: The dugong is a sea cow that eats seagrass.

49322.q: About how long is the Great Barrier Reef?
49322.e: The reef stretches for about 2,300 kilometres along the coast. That is much longer than the whole of Switzerland.
49322.m: The Great Barrier Reef is over 2,000 kilometres long.

49323.q: How big is the area of the Great Barrier Reef compared with Switzerland?
49323.e: The reef area covers about 344,000 square kilometres. Switzerland has about 41,000 square kilometres.
49323.m: The Great Barrier Reef is much bigger than Switzerland.

49324.q: Which famous list has the Great Barrier Reef been on since 1981?
a: List of the Wonders of the World
49324.e: In 1981 the Great Barrier Reef was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as a natural site.
49324.m: The Great Barrier Reef is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

49325.q: What harms the corals of the Great Barrier Reef most?
49325.e: If the seawater gets too warm, the corals become ill and can die. That has already happened many times on the Great Barrier Reef.
49325.m: Water that is too warm harms the corals of the reef.

49326.q: Which animal eats lots of corals on the Great Barrier Reef?
49326.e: The crown-of-thorns starfish has lots of spines and eats corals. When there are very many of them, they badly damage the reef.

49328.q: Which city is a well-known starting point for trips to the Great Barrier Reef?
49328.e: Cairns is in the north-east of Australia, right by the sea. Many boats go to the reef from there.
49328.m: Many boats go to the Great Barrier Reef from Cairns.

49329.e: Corals look like plants or stones. In fact they are small animals.

49330.q: In what kind of water do most coral reefs grow?
49330.e: Reef-building corals need warm seawater. That is why most reefs are in the tropics.
49330.m: Coral reefs grow in warm seas.

49331.q: What do corals build their hard skeleton from?
49331.e: Corals make limestone. Over time, many limestone skeletons together form a whole reef.
49331.m: Corals build their skeleton from limestone.

49332.q: What is it called when corals lose their colour and turn white?
49332.e: In coral bleaching, corals lose their colour. Then you can see their white skeleton.
49332.m: In coral bleaching, corals turn white.

49333.q: Which colourful fish nibbles at corals and makes fine white sand as it does so?
49333.e: The parrotfish has a mouth like a beak. It nibbles algae off the corals and passes out ground-up limestone as fine sand.
49333.m: Parrotfish make fine white sand on the reef.

49334.q: Why do coral reefs only grow where the sea is not deep?
a: They need sand from the beach
49334.e: Corals need lots of light to live. In deep water it is too dark.
49334.m: Reef corals need lots of sunlight.

49335.q: What is a ring-shaped coral reef with a lagoon in the middle called?
49335.e: An atoll is a ring of coral reefs and small islands. In the middle there is a lagoon.
49335.m: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef.

49336.q: What are coral reefs often called because so many kinds of animals live there?
49336.e: A huge variety of animals live in coral reefs. That is why they are compared with rainforests.
49336.m: Coral reefs are the rainforests of the sea.

49337.q: What is a single small coral animal called?
49337.e: A coral animal is called a polyp. Many polyps live together in a colony.
49337.m: A single coral animal is called a polyp.

49338.q: How long can a blue whale grow?
49338.e: Large blue whales grow to about 30 metres long. That is about as long as two buses one behind the other.
49338.m: A blue whale can grow to about 30 metres long.

49339.q: How heavy can a blue whale get?
49339.e: A large blue whale weighs well over 100 tonnes. That is as heavy as many elephants put together.
49339.m: A blue whale weighs over 100 tonnes.

49340.q: What does the blue whale mainly eat?
49340.e: The blue whale mainly eats krill. These are small crustaceans that live in huge swarms.
49340.m: The blue whale mainly eats small crustaceans called krill.

49341.q: Which group of animals does the blue whale belong to?
49341.e: Whales are mammals. They breathe air with lungs and feed their young on milk.
49341.m: The blue whale is a mammal, not a fish.

49342.q: What can you see when a blue whale breathes out at the surface?
a: Lots of air bubbles in the sand
49342.e: When breathing out, the blue whale blows warm, moist air upwards. This column is called a “blow” and can be about 9 metres high.
49342.m: When a whale breathes out, you see a tall column.

49343.q: What does the blue whale have in its mouth instead of teeth?
49343.e: Baleen is made of long plates of horn-like material. The whale uses it to sieve its food out of the water.
49343.m: The blue whale has baleen instead of teeth.

49344.q: About how long is a baby blue whale at birth?
49344.e: A newborn blue whale is already about 7 metres long. It weighs about as much as two cars.
49344.m: Even a baby blue whale is about 7 metres long.

49345.q: Why are there only a few blue whales left today?
a: They were heavily hunted in the past
49345.e: In the past a great many blue whales were hunted. Today they are protected, but there are still only a few.
49345.m: Blue whales are protected today because they were almost wiped out.

49346.q: What does a dolphin breathe through?
49346.e: Dolphins breathe air. To do so they come to the surface and breathe through the blowhole on top of their head.
49346.m: Dolphins breathe through the blowhole on their head.

49347.q: How do dolphins find their prey in murky water?
49347.e: Dolphins send out clicking sounds. The echo tells them where a fish is swimming.
49347.m: Dolphins locate prey with clicks and echoes.

a: With one half of the brain
49348.e: When they sleep, dolphins keep one half of the brain awake. That way they can keep breathing and watch out for danger.
49348.m: Dolphins always sleep with only one half of the brain.

49349.e: Dolphins usually live in groups. They hunt and play together.
49349.m: Dolphins like to live in groups.

49350.q: Which large sea mammal belongs to the dolphin family?
49350.e: The orca, also called the killer whale, is the largest dolphin. It is black and white.
49350.m: The orca is the largest dolphin.

49351.q: What is the best-known kind of dolphin called?
49351.e: The bottlenose dolphin is the best-known dolphin. It is grey and lives in many seas. The harbour porpoise, narwhal and beluga are other toothed whales.
49351.m: The bottlenose dolphin is the best-known dolphin.

49352.q: How do dolphins call each other?
49352.e: Every dolphin has its own whistle. It works almost like a name.
49352.m: Dolphins call each other with their own whistles.

49353.q: How does a dolphin move its tail fin when swimming?
49353.e: A dolphin's tail fin is horizontal. It beats it up and down, whereas a fish moves its tail from side to side.
49353.m: Dolphins beat their tail fin up and down.

49354.q: Apart from the sea, where else do dolphins live?
49354.e: There are river dolphins, for example in the Amazon in South America.

49355.q: Which fish is the largest fish in the world?
49355.e: The whale shark is the largest fish. It can grow to over 12 metres long.
49355.m: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world.

49356.q: What does the whale shark mainly eat?
49356.e: The whale shark filters tiny living things, called plankton, out of the water. It is harmless to people.
49356.m: The whale shark eats tiny plankton.

49357.q: What is a shark's skeleton made of?
49357.e: Sharks do not have a skeleton of bone, but one of cartilage. You have cartilage in your ears too.
49357.m: Sharks have a skeleton made of cartilage.

49358.q: How did the hammerhead shark get its name?
a: From the shape of its head
49358.e: The hammerhead shark's head is wide like a hammer. Its eyes are at the ends.
49358.m: The hammerhead shark has a head like a hammer.

49359.q: What is a shark especially good at?
a: Staying on land for a long time
49359.e: Sharks have a very good sense of smell. They notice even the tiniest traces in the water.
49359.m: Sharks have a very keen nose.

49360.q: How often do sharks attack people?
a: Every time someone swims in the sea
49360.e: Shark attacks on people are very rare. Sharks are caught by people far more often.
49360.m: Sharks only very rarely attack people.

49361.q: Since when have there been sharks on Earth?
49361.e: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years. The first dinosaurs lived much later.
49361.m: There were sharks even before the dinosaurs.

49362.q: What do sea turtles breathe with?
49362.e: Sea turtles are reptiles and breathe with lungs. They have to come to the surface to breathe.
49362.m: Sea turtles come up to the surface for air.

49363.q: How many species of sea turtle are there?
49363.e: There are seven species of sea turtle. Almost all of them are endangered.
49363.m: There are seven species of sea turtle.

49364.q: What decides whether a female or a male hatches from a sea turtle egg?
49364.e: If the sand is warmer, more females hatch. If it is cooler, more males hatch.
49364.m: The warmth of the sand decides whether a female hatches.

49365.q: Why do sea turtles sometimes eat plastic bags?
a: They use them to clean the sea
They build a nest with them
49365.e: A plastic bag in the water looks like a jellyfish. The plastic can make the turtle ill.
49365.m: Plastic in the sea is dangerous for turtles.

49366.q: What is the largest sea turtle called?
49366.e: The leatherback turtle grows to about 2 metres long. Its shell is covered with leathery skin.
49366.m: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle.

49367.q: What can a sea turtle not do that many tortoises can?
49367.e: Sea turtles cannot pull their head and legs into their shell. But they are nimble swimmers.
49367.m: Sea turtles cannot pull in their head.

49368.q: What do sea turtles have instead of feet with toes?
49368.e: Their legs have become wide flippers. With them they can swim well.

49369.q: Where do newly hatched sea turtles crawl to?
49369.e: The little turtles dig their way out of the sand. Then they hurry to the sea as fast as they can.
49369.m: Young sea turtles crawl straight to the sea.

49370.q: Where do female sea turtles often return to lay their eggs?
a: To the beach where they were born
49370.e: Many females swim thousands of kilometres back. They often lay their eggs on the beach where they hatched themselves.
49370.m: Sea turtles find their way back to the beach where they were born.

49371.q: Which animal does the clownfish live in?
49371.e: The clownfish lives between the tentacles of a sea anemone. There it is safe from enemies.
49371.m: The clownfish lives in a sea anemone.

49372.q: Why does the clownfish not get stung by the tentacles of the animal it lives in?
a: A layer of slime protects it
49372.e: The clownfish has a special layer of slime on its skin. That is why the tentacles do not sting it.
49372.m: A layer of slime protects the clownfish.

49373.q: What colours is the well-known clownfish?
49373.e: The best-known clownfish is orange with white stripes. The stripes often have a black edge.
49373.m: The clownfish is orange with white stripes.

49374.q: In which animated film is a clownfish the main character?
49374.e: In the film “Finding Nemo”, a clownfish dad searches the sea for his son Nemo.

49375.q: What happens with clownfish when the female of a group dies?
a: The largest male becomes a female
The young grow up at once
49375.e: Clownfish can change from male to female. The largest male then becomes the new female.
49375.m: Clownfish can change from male to female.

49376.q: Where do clownfish live in the wild?
a: In cold seas near the ice
49376.e: Clownfish live in warm coral reefs in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific.

49377.q: About how big does a clownfish grow?
49377.e: Clownfish are small fish. Most grow to about 10 centimetres long.
49377.m: A clownfish is about as long as a finger.

49378.q: How does the clownfish help the animal it lives in?
a: It keeps it warm in winter
49378.e: The clownfish chases away fish that want to eat its host. Both animals help each other.
49378.m: The clownfish and its host help each other.

49379.q: Who mainly guards the eggs in clownfish?
49379.e: With clownfish it is mainly the father who looks after the eggs. He fans fresh water over them.
49379.m: With clownfish, the father guards the eggs.

49380.q: Why is it dark in the deep sea?
a: Sunlight does not reach that deep
The fish switch off the light
49380.e: Sunlight only gets a few hundred metres down into the sea. Below that it is pitch dark.
49380.m: The deep sea is dark because no sunlight gets there.

49381.q: What can many animals in the deep sea make themselves?
49381.e: Many deep-sea animals can glow. That is how they lure prey or find a partner.
49381.m: Many deep-sea animals can glow on their own.

49382.q: Which deep-sea fish lures prey with a glowing fishing rod on its head?
49382.e: The anglerfish has a kind of fishing rod with a glowing bait on its head. When a fish comes closer, it snaps it up.
49382.m: The anglerfish fishes with a glowing bait.

49383.q: How cold is the water in the deep sea usually?
a: Only a few degrees above zero
49383.e: The sun only warms the water at the top. Almost everywhere in the deep sea it is only a few degrees.
49383.m: The water in the deep sea is very cold.

49384.q: What drifts slowly down in the deep sea and is food for many animals?
49384.e: Marine snow is made of tiny remains of dead animals and plants. They sink slowly and look like snowflakes.
49384.m: Many deep-sea animals live on marine snow.

49385.q: What presses very hard on everything in the deep sea?
49385.e: There is a huge amount of water above the deep sea. Its weight presses on everything with great force.
49385.m: The water pressure in the deep sea is enormous.

49386.q: Which animal with long tentacles lives in the deep sea?
49386.e: The giant squid is a kind of cephalopod. With its tentacles it can be about 10 metres long, and it has huge eyes.
49386.m: The giant squid lives in the deep sea.

49387.q: Which whale dives especially deep to hunt squid?
49387.e: The sperm whale can dive over 1,000 metres deep. There it hunts squid.
49387.m: The sperm whale is a record-breaking diver.

49388.q: What is there in some places on the floor of the deep sea?
49388.e: In some places hot water streams out of the seabed. They are also called “black smokers”. Special animals such as tube worms live there.
49388.m: There are hot springs on the deep-sea floor.

49389.q: What is a jellyfish mostly made of?
49389.e: A jellyfish is about 98 per cent water. That is why it is so see-through and soft.
49389.m: Jellyfish are made almost entirely of water.

49390.q: What does a jellyfish not have?
49390.e: Jellyfish have no brain. They only have a simple network of nerves.

49391.q: What do jellyfish catch their prey with?
49391.e: The tentacles have stinging cells with venom. Jellyfish use them to paralyse small animals.
49391.m: Jellyfish catch prey with their stings.

49392.e: The jellyfish squeezes its bell together, pushing water out. That moves it forward.
49392.m: Jellyfish swim by squeezing their bell together.

49393.q: Which jellyfish can turn back into a young form?
49393.e: When in danger, the immortal jellyfish can turn back into a young polyp. Then it grows up all over again.
49393.m: The immortal jellyfish can become young again.

49394.q: The moon jellyfish also lives in the North Sea. What does it look like?
a: See-through with four rings in the middle
49394.e: The moon jellyfish has four ring-shaped patterns in the middle. It is also common in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
49394.m: The moon jellyfish has four rings in the middle.

49395.q: Which jellyfish is one of the largest jellyfish in the world?
49395.e: The lion's mane jellyfish often has a bell about a metre wide, in rare cases over 2 metres. Its tentacles are very long.
49395.m: The lion's mane jellyfish is a giant jellyfish.

49396.q: Which jellyfish is thought to be one of the most venomous animals in the sea?
49396.e: The box jellyfish, also called the sea wasp, lives mainly off Australia. Its venom is very strong and dangerous to people.
49396.m: The box jellyfish is a very venomous jellyfish.

49397.q: Are there jellyfish in Swiss lakes too?
49397.e: A small freshwater jellyfish lives in some Swiss lakes. It is only about 2 centimetres big, harmless to people and appears mainly in summer.
49397.m: There are small jellyfish in Swiss lakes too.

49398.e: Mangroves are trees and shrubs. They grow on tropical coasts right by the sea.
49398.m: Mangroves are trees by the sea.

49399.q: What do the roots of many mangroves look like?
49399.e: Many mangroves stand on stilt roots. That way they hold on in the soft mud.

49400.q: What kind of water can mangroves cope with?
49400.e: Most trees die in salt water. But mangroves can cope well with the salt.

49401.q: Why are mangroves important for many young fish?
a: As a feeding place for whales
As a sleeping place for birds
49401.e: Young fish can hide well between the roots. Large predators find it hard to get in there.
49401.m: Mangroves are a nursery for fish.

49402.q: How do mangroves protect the coast?
a: They slow down waves and storm surges
49402.e: The dense roots slow down the waves. That way the coast is damaged less during storms.
49402.m: Mangroves protect the coast from waves.

a: Where the tide comes in and goes out
In the middle of the desert
49403.e: Mangroves grow at the edge of the sea. At high tide they stand in water, at low tide in mud.
49403.m: Mangroves grow where the tide comes and goes.

49404.q: Which large predator lives in the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans in Asia?
49404.e: The Sundarbans in Bangladesh and India are a huge mangrove forest. The Bengal tiger, also called the royal Bengal tiger, lives there.
49404.m: Tigers live in the mangroves of the Sundarbans.

49405.q: The mudskipper is a fish from the mangroves. What can it do?
a: Blow itself up like a ball
Spend the winter under the ice
49405.e: The mudskipper can stay on land for a while. It hops across the mud with its front fins.
49405.m: The mudskipper hops across the mud.

49406.q: What is special about the seeds of some mangroves?
a: They sprout while still on the tree
49406.e: In some mangroves the seeds already sprout on the tree. Then the young plants drop off and carry on growing in the mud.
49406.m: Some mangrove seeds sprout while still on the tree.

49407.q: How many arms do most starfish have?
49407.e: Most starfish have five arms. But there are also kinds with many more arms.

49408.q: Where are a starfish's simple eyes?
a: At the tips of its arms
49408.e: There is a simple eye at the tip of each arm. With it the starfish can tell light from dark.
49408.m: Starfish see with the tips of their arms.

49409.q: How does a starfish eat a mussel?
a: It pushes its stomach out of its body
It cracks it open with its teeth
It sucks it up with a trunk
49409.e: The starfish pulls the mussel's shell open a crack. Then it pushes its stomach inside and digests it.
49409.m: The starfish digests its prey with its stomach outside its body.

49410.e: On the underside of its arms the starfish has many tiny tube feet with suckers. It crawls slowly with them.

49411.q: Which group of animals do starfish belong to?
49411.e: Starfish are not fish. They belong to the echinoderms, which means “spiny skins”, because their skin often has small spines.

49412.q: Which animal is a close relative of the starfish?
49412.e: The sea urchin is related to the starfish. Both have a body divided into five equal parts.
49412.m: Sea urchins and starfish are relatives.

a: At the tip of an arm
49413.e: A starfish's mouth is on its underside, right in the middle.
49413.m: The starfish has its mouth on its underside.

49414.e: Starfish need salt water. That is why they only live in the sea and never in lakes or rivers.
49414.m: Starfish only live in the salty sea.

49415.q: Which sea borders Egypt to the north?
49415.e: Egypt's north coast is on the Mediterranean. The city of Alexandria is there too.
49415.m: The Mediterranean lies to the north of Egypt.

49416.q: Which sea lies to the east of Egypt?
49416.e: In the east Egypt has a long coast on the Red Sea. There are colourful coral reefs there.
49416.m: The Red Sea lies to the east of Egypt.

49417.q: Which desert does most of Egypt belong to?
49417.e: Egypt is mostly desert. It is part of the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world.
49417.m: Most of Egypt is desert and belongs to the Sahara.

49418.q: About how many people live in Egypt (as of 2024)?
49418.e: Over 100 million people live in Egypt. That is more than ten times as many as in Switzerland.
49418.m: Over 100 million people live in Egypt.

49419.q: Which famous canal for ships is in Egypt?
49419.e: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Thanks to it, ships travelling between Europe and Asia no longer have to sail all the way round Africa.
49419.m: The Suez Canal in Egypt is an important shortcut for ships.

49420.q: Which animal was sacred in ancient Egypt and was even buried as a mummy?
49420.e: Cats were greatly honoured in ancient Egypt. Many cat mummies have been found.
49420.m: In ancient Egypt cats were sacred animals.

49421.q: Which young pharaoh became famous because of his tomb with a golden mask?
49421.e: Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered in 1922 in the Valley of the Kings. Inside was a magnificent death mask made of gold.
49421.m: Tutankhamun is famous for his golden death mask.

49422.q: What is the capital of Morocco?
49422.e: The capital of Morocco is Rabat. The king lives there and the government works there.
49422.m: Rabat is the capital of Morocco.

49423.q: Which city is the largest city in Morocco?
49423.e: Casablanca is the largest city in Morocco. It has a big port on the Atlantic.
49423.m: Casablanca is the largest city in Morocco.

49424.q: The old town of Chefchaouen in Morocco is famous for its colour. What colour are many of the houses there?
49424.e: In Chefchaouen many houses and alleys are painted light blue. That is why it is also called “the blue city”.
49424.m: Chefchaouen in Morocco is the blue city.

49425.q: Which strait separates Morocco from Spain?
49425.e: The Strait of Gibraltar lies between Morocco and Spain. At its narrowest point it is only about 14 kilometres wide.
49425.m: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Africa from Europe.

49426.q: Who is the head of state in Morocco?
49426.e: Morocco is a kingdom. A king is at the head of the state.
49426.m: Morocco is a kingdom with a king.

49427.q: Which city in Morocco is called “the Red City”?
49427.e: Many houses and walls in Marrakesh are built of reddish clay. That is why it is called “the Red City”.
49427.m: Marrakesh is called “the Red City” because of its reddish walls.

49428.q: Which ocean lies along the west coast of Morocco?
49428.e: Morocco's long west coast is on the Atlantic Ocean. There are many surfing beaches there.
49428.m: Morocco has a coast on the Atlantic to the west.
